worked.short: $n(\mathrm{HCl})_{\mathrm{titre}}=0.00200$ mol; $n(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3)_{\mathrm{aliquot}}=0.00100$ mol; $n(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3)_{\mathrm{whole}}=0.0100$ mol. The requested mass is $0.0100\times106.0=1.06$ g.
worked.saving: The labels show exactly where the aliquot must be scaled to the whole solution.

pitfalls: Reporting the aliquot amount when the question asks for the whole solution.
Applying the volume ratio before identifying which substance the amount refers to.
Reporting $M_r$ as though it were the requested mass.
SEM-9701-carry-a-named-quantity-through-.check: The whole-solution amount must be $250/25.0=10$ times the aliquot amount in the worked question.

practice.stem: A $250$ cm$^3$ solution contains sodium carbonate. A $25.0$ cm$^3$ aliquot requires $25.0$ cm$^3$ of $0.120$ mol dm$^{-3}$ HCl for complete neutralisation. One mole of sodium carbonate reacts with two moles of HCl. Find the mass of sodium carbonate in the whole solution, in g to $3$ significant figures. Use $M_r(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3)=106.0$.
hints: The titre gives an HCl amount, but the question asks about the whole solution.
Name the HCl amount in the titre and the sodium carbonate amounts in the aliquot and whole solution.
practice.explanation: $n(\mathrm{HCl})_{\mathrm{titre}}=0.120\times25.0/1000=0.00300$ mol. Thus $n(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3)_{\mathrm{aliquot}}=0.00150$ mol and $n(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3)_{\mathrm{whole}}=0.00150\times250/25.0=0.0150$ mol. The mass is $0.0150\times106.0=1.59$ g.
practice.shortcut_use: Name each amount before scaling the aliquot.

practice.stem: A $100$ cm$^3$ solution contains sodium hydroxide. A $25.0$ cm$^3$ aliquot requires $20.0$ cm$^3$ of $0.0750$ mol dm$^{-3}$ sulfuric acid for complete neutralisation. One mole of sulfuric acid reacts with two moles of sodium hydroxide. Find the mass of sodium hydroxide in the whole solution, in g to $3$ significant figures. Use $M_r(\mathrm{NaOH})=40.0$.
hints: The measured titre contains sulfuric acid; the requested mass is for sodium hydroxide in the whole solution.
Use the reaction ratio to name the sodium hydroxide amount in the aliquot, then scale it to the whole solution.
practice.explanation: $n(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4)_{\mathrm{titre}}=0.0750\times20.0/1000=0.00150$ mol. Thus $n(\mathrm{NaOH})_{\mathrm{aliquot}}=0.00300$ mol and $n(\mathrm{NaOH})_{\mathrm{whole}}=0.00300\times100/25.0=0.0120$ mol. The mass is $0.0120\times40.0=0.480$ g.
practice.shortcut_use: Track the named amount through the reaction ratio and sample scaling.

recall.q: What two details should an intermediate amount name carry?
recall.a: It should name the substance and the sample or location.

recall.q: When can an aliquot amount be scaled to a whole solution?
recall.a: When the aliquot represents the whole solution.

recall.q: What should the final label match?
recall.a: It should match both the substance and sample size requested.

SEM-9701-average.hook: Adding isotope masses or using an ordinary mean ignores how common each isotope is.
SEM-9701-average.when: Isotope masses are paired with percentage abundances or relative peak heights.
SEM-9701-average.why: Each mass contributes in proportion to its abundance. This holds when the abundances or peak heights represent the relative amounts of the isotopes.
steps: Multiply each isotope mass by its abundance.
Add those products.
Divide by the sum of the abundances.

worked.question: An element has isotopes of mass 10 and 11 with relative peak heights 1 and 4. Find its $A_r$.
worked.long: One atom of mass 10 and four of mass 11 have mean mass $(10+11+11+11+11)/5=10.8$.
worked.saving: Weights the isotopes without expanding the peaks into individual atoms.

pitfalls: Taking the ordinary mean of the isotope masses.
Dividing by 100 when the abundances are relative peak heights that do not total 100.
SEM-9701-average.check: The answer must lie between the lightest and heaviest isotope masses.

practice.stem: Isotopes of mass 20 and 22 have relative peak heights 3 and 1. Find $A_r$ as a bare number.
hints: The heights give relative abundances.
Weight each mass by its height.
Set up $(20\times3+22\times1)/(3+1)$.
practice.shortcut_use: Use peak heights directly as weights.

practice.stem: Isotopes of mass 35 and 37 have abundances 75% and 25%. Find $A_r$ as a bare number.
hints: The isotope abundances are unequal.
Use a weighted mean.
practice.shortcut_use: Weight each isotope by its percentage abundance.

recall.q: What is the weighted-mean formula for $A_r$?
recall.a: Divide the sum of abundance times isotope mass by the sum of abundances.

recall.q: Can relative peak heights be used as abundances?
recall.a: Yes, when they represent the relative amounts of the isotopes.

SEM-9701-gas-volumes-same-and.hook: Converting every gas volume to moles adds calculation when only a reaction ratio is needed.
SEM-9701-gas-volumes-same-and.when: Reacting gases and products are measured at the same temperature and pressure.
SEM-9701-gas-volumes-same-and.idea: At the same temperature and pressure, gas volume ratio equals mole ratio.
SEM-9701-gas-volumes-same-and.why: Equal gas volumes contain equal numbers of molecules at the same temperature and pressure. Use this only for gas volumes measured under those same conditions; liquid water has no gas-volume coefficient.
steps: Write the balanced equation.
Read coefficients for gaseous substances.
Use those coefficients as volume ratios.
Exclude liquids from the gas-volume comparison.

worked.question: At the same temperature and pressure, 20 cm$^3$ of methane burns completely in 40 cm$^3$ of oxygen. What volume of carbon dioxide forms? Water is liquid after cooling.
worked.long: Convert both gas volumes to moles using a common molar gas volume, use $\mathrm{CH_4}+2\mathrm{O_2}\to\mathrm{CO_2}+2\mathrm{H_2O}$, then convert carbon dioxide moles back to volume: 20 cm$^3$.
worked.short: $\mathrm{CH_4}:\mathrm{CO_2}=1:1$, so 20 cm$^3$ methane gives 20 cm$^3$ carbon dioxide.
worked.saving: Cancels the common molar gas volume.

pitfalls: Comparing volumes measured at different temperatures or pressures.
Including liquid water as a gas volume.
Using oxygen supplied instead of oxygen used when oxygen is in excess.
SEM-9701-gas-volumes-same-and.check: The gas-volume ratio should match the gaseous coefficients in the balanced equation.

practice.stem: At the same temperature and pressure, 15 cm$^3$ of ethene burns completely. For $\mathrm{C_2H_4}+3\mathrm{O_2}\to2\mathrm{CO_2}+2\mathrm{H_2O}$, find the volume of carbon dioxide in cm$^3$.
hints: All stated gas volumes share the same conditions.
Use the ethene-to-carbon-dioxide coefficient ratio.
Set up $V_{\mathrm{CO_2}}=15\times2/1$.
practice.explanation: The gas-volume ratio $\mathrm{C_2H_4}:\mathrm{CO_2}$ is $1:2$, so $15\times2=30$ cm$^3$.
practice.shortcut_use: Replace mole ratio with gas-volume ratio.

practice.stem: At the same temperature and pressure, 24 cm$^3$ of propane burns completely. For $\mathrm{C_3H_8}+5\mathrm{O_2}\to3\mathrm{CO_2}+4\mathrm{H_2O}$, find the oxygen volume used in cm$^3$.
hints: Look at the propane-to-oxygen coefficients.
Apply that ratio directly to volumes.
Set up $V_{\mathrm{O_2}}=24\times5/1$.
practice.explanation: The gas-volume ratio $\mathrm{C_3H_8}:\mathrm{O_2}$ is $1:5$, so the oxygen used is $24\times5=120$ cm$^3$.
practice.shortcut_use: Use coefficients directly as gas-volume ratios.

recall.q: When does gas volume ratio equal mole ratio?
recall.a: When the gas volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

recall.q: Why is liquid water excluded from a gas-volume ratio?
recall.a: Its liquid volume does not follow the gaseous coefficient ratio.

SEM-9701-ionic-equations.hook: A full equation can hide which ions actually change.
SEM-9701-ionic-equations.when: An aqueous reaction includes ionic compounds and asks for a net ionic equation.
SEM-9701-ionic-equations.idea: Write the full equation, split aqueous ionic compounds into ions, then cancel identical spectator ions.
SEM-9701-ionic-equations.why: Spectator ions appear unchanged on both sides and contribute no net chemical change. Splitting applies to aqueous ionic compounds; keep solids, liquids and non-ionic substances intact.
steps: Write and balance the full equation.
Split aqueous ionic compounds into ions.
Cancel identical ions on both sides.
Check atoms and charge in the remaining equation.

worked.question: Aqueous silver nitrate reacts with aqueous sodium chloride to form solid silver chloride and aqueous sodium nitrate. Write the net ionic equation.
worked.long: $\mathrm{AgNO_3(aq)}+\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}\to\mathrm{AgCl(s)}+\mathrm{NaNO_3(aq)}$; expand all aqueous ionic compounds and compare both sides.
worked.short: Cancel $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ after splitting: $\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)}+\mathrm{Cl^-(aq)}\to\mathrm{AgCl(s)}$.
worked.saving: Shows the precipitate-forming ions without carrying spectators.

pitfalls: Splitting a solid precipitate into ions.
Cancelling ions whose amounts or forms differ across the equation.
Leaving spectator ions in the final equation.
SEM-9701-ionic-equations.check: Both atom counts and total charge must balance.

practice.stem: Aqueous barium chloride reacts with aqueous sodium sulfate to form solid barium sulfate and aqueous sodium chloride. Give the net ionic equation.
hints: The solid is the product that stays intact.
Split the aqueous ionic compounds.
Cancel $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ from both sides.
practice.explanation: The sodium and chloride ions are spectators, leaving $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}(aq)}+\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)}\to\mathrm{BaSO_4(s)}$.
practice.shortcut_use: Cancel unchanged aqueous ions.

practice.stem: Aqueous hydrochloric acid reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form liquid water and aqueous sodium chloride. Give the net ionic equation.
hints: Identify the liquid product.
Split the aqueous ionic substances.
Cancel $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ from both sides.
practice.explanation: Sodium and chloride ions are unchanged, so the net equation is $\mathrm{H^+(aq)}+\mathrm{OH^-(aq)}\to\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$.
practice.shortcut_use: Remove spectator ions after splitting.

recall.q: Which substances are split when writing a net ionic equation?
recall.a: Split aqueous ionic compounds into their ions.

recall.q: What makes an ion a spectator?
recall.a: It appears unchanged on both sides of the equation.

SEM-9701-keep-the-aliquot-fraction-visib.hook: A reaction ratio and a dilution factor can be confused when both appear in one calculation.
SEM-9701-keep-the-aliquot-fraction-visib.when: Only an aliquot of a larger, uniform stock solution is analysed.
SEM-9701-keep-the-aliquot-fraction-visib.why: A uniform solution has the same concentration in the aliquot and stock, so amount is proportional to volume. This holds when the aliquot is representative of the stock solution.
steps: Find moles in the aliquot from the reaction.
Write the stock-to-aliquot volume ratio.
Multiply the aliquot amount by that ratio.
Check that the stock amount is larger.

worked.question: A 25.0 cm$^3$ aliquot from a uniform 250.0 cm$^3$ stock contains 0.00200 mol of solute. Find the moles in the stock.
worked.long: The concentration is $0.00200/25.0=0.0000800$ mol cm$^{-3}$; multiply by 250.0 cm$^3$ to get 0.0200 mol.
worked.saving: Avoids a separate concentration calculation and exposes the factor of ten.

pitfalls: Multiplying by $V_a/V_s$ instead of $V_s/V_a$.
Applying the volume factor before finding the aliquot's solute amount from the reaction.
Using the ratio when the aliquot is not representative of the stock.
SEM-9701-keep-the-aliquot-fraction-visib.check: Since $V_s>V_a$, the stock must contain more solute than the aliquot.

practice.stem: A 20.0 cm$^3$ aliquot from a uniform 100.0 cm$^3$ stock contains 0.00300 mol of solute. Find the moles in the stock.
hints: The stock and aliquot have the same concentration.
Use the stock-volume-to-aliquot-volume ratio.
practice.shortcut_use: Scale aliquot moles by the volume ratio.

practice.stem: A 10.0 cm$^3$ aliquot from a uniform 250.0 cm$^3$ stock reacts with 0.00400 mol of acid. Each mole of solute reacts with 2 mol of acid. Find the moles of solute in the stock.
hints: First find solute moles in the aliquot from the reaction ratio.
Then use the stock-to-aliquot volume ratio.
practice.explanation: The aliquot has $0.00400/2=0.00200$ mol of solute; the stock has $0.00200(250.0/10.0)=0.0500$ mol.
practice.shortcut_use: Keep reaction ratio and aliquot scaling on separate lines.

recall.q: How are stock and aliquot amounts related for a uniform solution?
recall.a: $n_{\mathrm{stock}}=n_{\mathrm{aliquot}}(V_s/V_a)$.

recall.q: What quick size check applies when $V_s>V_a$?
recall.a: The stock amount must exceed the aliquot amount.

SEM-9701-limiting-reagent.hook: Comparing reagent mole amounts alone fails when the equation uses different coefficients.
SEM-9701-limiting-reagent.when: Amounts of two or more reactants are given and you must identify the one used up first.
SEM-9701-limiting-reagent.idea: Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient; the smallest result identifies the limiting reagent.
SEM-9701-limiting-reagent.why: Each quotient is the number of complete reaction batches that reactant can supply. This holds for a balanced equation when the stated reactants react according to it.
steps: Balance the equation.
Divide each reactant amount by its coefficient.
Choose the smaller quotient.
Use that quotient to find product amounts.

worked.question: For $\mathrm{N_2}+3\mathrm{H_2}\to2\mathrm{NH_3}$, 2.0 mol of $\mathrm{N_2}$ reacts with 3.0 mol of $\mathrm{H_2}$. Identify the limiting reagent and find the moles of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ formed.
worked.long: Using all 2.0 mol of $\mathrm{N_2}$ would need 6.0 mol of $\mathrm{H_2}$, but only 3.0 mol is available; this forms 2.0 mol of $\mathrm{NH_3}$.
worked.short: $2.0/1=2.0$ and $3.0/3=1.0$, so $\mathrm{H_2}$ limits the reaction to 1.0 batch, forming $1.0\times2=2.0$ mol of $\mathrm{NH_3}$.
worked.saving: Identifies the limiting reagent without calculating each reactant's full demand.

pitfalls: Choosing the reactant with fewer moles without using coefficients.
Using coefficients from an unbalanced equation.
Calculating product from an excess reactant.
SEM-9701-limiting-reagent.check: The predicted reaction cannot use more of either reactant than was supplied.

practice.stem: For $\mathrm{2Al}+3\mathrm{Cl_2}\to2\mathrm{AlCl_3}$, 4.0 mol of Al and 3.0 mol of $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ are supplied. Which reactant is limiting?

options.A: Neither; they are in the exact reaction ratio.
options.B: Al, because its coefficient is smaller.

hints: Compare reaction batches available.
Divide each amount by its own coefficient.
Compare $4.0/2$ with $3.0/3$.
practice.explanation: Al supplies $4.0/2=2.0$ batches, while $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ supplies $3.0/3=1.0$ batch. $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ is limiting.
practice.shortcut_use: Compare moles divided by coefficients.

practice.stem: For $\mathrm{N_2}+3\mathrm{H_2}\to2\mathrm{NH_3}$, 1.5 mol of $\mathrm{N_2}$ and 6.0 mol of $\mathrm{H_2}$ are supplied. Find the moles of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ formed.
hints: Find how many reaction batches each reagent supplies.
Divide each amount by its coefficient.
Compare $1.5/1$ with $6.0/3$, then multiply the smaller result by the product coefficient.
practice.explanation: $1.5/1=1.5$ batches and $6.0/3=2.0$ batches, so $\mathrm{N_2}$ limits the reaction. Ammonia formed is $1.5\times2=3.0$ mol.
practice.shortcut_use: Use the smaller moles-per-coefficient quotient.

recall.q: How do you identify the limiting reagent from amounts and coefficients?
recall.a: Divide each reagent's moles by its coefficient and choose the smallest quotient.

recall.q: What does moles divided by coefficient represent?
recall.a: It represents the number of reaction batches that reagent can supply.

SEM-9701-back-titration-subtraction-line.hook: The titration measures reagent left over. Treating that amount as reagent consumed gives the wrong amount of analyte.
SEM-9701-back-titration-subtraction-line.when: An excess reagent is added to a sample, and the remainder is measured by titration.
SEM-9701-back-titration-subtraction-line.idea: Write $n_{\mathrm{reacted}}=n_{\mathrm{added}}-n_{\mathrm{remaining}}$ before using reaction coefficients or an aliquot factor.
SEM-9701-back-titration-subtraction-line.why: The added reagent is either consumed by the sample or remains for titration, provided these are its only reactions. The titration amount must represent the whole remainder before subtraction.
steps: Find moles of reagent added.
Use the titre to find moles remaining in the whole mixture.
Subtract remaining from added.
Use the reaction ratio to find moles of analyte.

worked.question: A sample of calcium carbonate reacts with $50.0$ mL of $0.200$ mol L$^{-1}$ HCl. The remaining acid requires $20.0$ mL of $0.100$ mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH for neutralisation. Find the amount of calcium carbonate in mol. One mole of calcium carbonate reacts with two moles of HCl.
worked.long: The initial acid is $0.0100$ mol and the titration accounts for $0.00200$ mol. The sample therefore consumes $0.00800$ mol of acid, equivalent to $0.00400$ mol of calcium carbonate.
worked.saving: Subtracting first prevents the reaction ratio being applied to the leftover acid.

pitfalls: Using the titre as the amount that reacted with the sample.
Applying the reaction coefficient before subtracting.
Forgetting to scale an aliquot titre to the whole mixture.
SEM-9701-back-titration-subtraction-line.check: The calculated remainder must be smaller than the amount added, giving a positive amount of analyte.

practice.stem: A calcium carbonate sample reacts with $40.0$ mL of $0.250$ mol L$^{-1}$ HCl. The remaining acid requires $25.0$ mL of $0.100$ mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH. One mole of calcium carbonate reacts with two moles of HCl. Find the amount of calcium carbonate in mol, to $3$ significant figures.
hints: The titre measures the acid left over.
Find the acid added and the acid remaining, then subtract.
Only after subtraction, use the $2:1$ acid-to-carbonate ratio.
practice.shortcut_use: Subtract the remaining acid before applying the reaction ratio.

practice.stem: A magnesium oxide sample reacts with $25.0$ mL of $0.400$ mol L$^{-1}$ HCl. The whole mixture is made up to $100.0$ mL. A $25.0$ mL aliquot requires $10.0$ mL of $0.100$ mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH to neutralise its remaining acid. One mole of magnesium oxide reacts with two moles of HCl. Find the amount of magnesium oxide in mol, to $3$ significant figures.
hints: The titre covers only an aliquot of the mixture.
Scale its acid amount to the whole mixture before subtracting.
The whole mixture is four times the aliquot; subtract its remaining acid from the added acid, then use the $2:1$ ratio.
practice.explanation: Acid added is $(0.0250)(0.400)=0.0100$ mol. Acid remaining in the whole mixture is $4(0.0100)(0.100)=0.00400$ mol. Thus $n(\mathrm{MgO})=(0.0100-0.00400)/2=0.00300$ mol. The answer is $0.00300$.
practice.shortcut_use: Scale the remainder, subtract it, then apply the reaction ratio.

recall.q: What subtraction starts a back-titration calculation?
recall.a: Moles reacted equal moles added minus moles remaining.

recall.q: When do you apply the reaction coefficient?
recall.a: Apply it after finding the moles of reagent that reacted.

recall.q: What must be done if the titre uses an aliquot?
recall.a: Scale the titrated remainder to the whole mixture before subtracting.

SEM-9701-balancing-redox-quickly.hook: Balancing atoms first can hide an electron mismatch. Oxidation-number changes reveal the required ratio before the water and acid terms are added.
SEM-9701-balancing-redox-quickly.when: A redox equation in acidic solution gives the reacting ions and asks for balanced coefficients.
SEM-9701-balancing-redox-quickly.idea: For each changing element, multiply its oxidation-number change by its number of atoms to count electrons. Equalise electron loss and gain; then balance O with $\mathrm{H_2O}$, H with $\mathrm{H^+}$, and charge with $e^-$ in half-equations.
SEM-9701-balancing-redox-quickly.why: Electrons lost must equal electrons gained. This method applies when the stated species react in acidic solution, where $\mathrm{H_2O}$ and $\mathrm{H^+}$ can balance O and H; the electrons cancel in the combined equation.
steps: Identify the atoms whose oxidation numbers change.
Count electrons lost and gained, including the number of each atom.
Multiply half-equations to equalise electrons.
Balance O with water and H with $\mathrm{H^+}$, then check charge and cancel electrons.

worked.question: In acidic solution, dichromate ions, $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$, oxidise $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ to $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ and are reduced to $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$. Find the smallest whole-number coefficient of $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ in the balanced equation.
worked.long: Balance separate half-equations. The dichromate half-equation uses $14\mathrm{H^+}$, $7\mathrm{H_2O}$ and $6e^-$; the iron half-equation releases one electron, so it must be multiplied by $6$.
worked.short: Each chromium changes from $+6$ to $+3$; two chromium atoms gain $2(3)=6$ electrons. Each iron loses one, so $6$ iron ions are needed. Balancing O and H then gives $7\mathrm{H_2O}$ and $14\mathrm{H^+}$.
worked.saving: The electron count fixes the iron coefficient before the rest of the equation is balanced.

pitfalls: Counting the change for one chromium atom but forgetting there are two in dichromate.
Using $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$ as though the solution were acidic when it is not stated to be.
Leaving electrons in the final combined equation.
SEM-9701-balancing-redox-quickly.check: Check both atom counts and total charge on each side; electrons must cancel.

practice.stem: In acidic solution, $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ is reduced to $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$. What is the coefficient of $\mathrm{H_2O}$ in the balanced reduction half-equation? Give the smallest whole number.
hints: Oxygen appears in the reactant ion but not in the stated manganese product.
Use water on the product side to balance oxygen.
After balancing oxygen, use $\mathrm{H^+}$ for hydrogen and electrons for charge.
practice.explanation: The oxygen atoms in $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ require $4\mathrm{H_2O}$ on the product side. Completing the half-equation gives $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ with $8\mathrm{H^+}$ and $5e^-$ forming $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ and $4\mathrm{H_2O}$. The answer is $4$.
practice.shortcut_use: Balance oxygen with water after identifying the reduction.

practice.stem: In acidic solution, $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ is reduced to $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ while $\mathrm{NO_2^-}$ is oxidised to $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$. Find the smallest whole-number coefficient of $\mathrm{NO_2^-}$ in the combined equation.
hints: Compare the oxidation-number changes of manganese and nitrogen.
Equalise electrons gained and lost before balancing oxygen and hydrogen.
Find the smallest common electron count, then use it to set the nitrite-to-permanganate ratio.
practice.explanation: Manganese changes from $+7$ to $+2$, gaining $5$ electrons; nitrogen changes from $+3$ to $+5$, losing $2$. Equalising at $10$ electrons requires $5\mathrm{NO_2^-}$ for $2\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$. The answer is $5$.
practice.shortcut_use: Use oxidation-number changes to fix the reactant ratio.

recall.q: How do you count electrons for an element whose oxidation number changes?
recall.a: Multiply its oxidation-number change by the number of its atoms.

recall.q: What must match between oxidation and reduction half-equations?
recall.a: Electrons lost must equal electrons gained.

recall.q: Which species balance O and H in an acidic half-equation?
recall.a: Use $\mathrm{H_2O}$ for O and $\mathrm{H^+}$ for H.

SEM-9701-mass-spectrometry.hook: Reading an isotope pattern peak by peak is slow, and confusing $M+1$ with $M+2$ can misidentify the element.
SEM-9701-mass-spectrometry.when: A molecular-ion cluster gives the heights of $M$ and $M+1$, or shows peaks at $M$, $M+2$ and possibly $M+4$.
SEM-9701-mass-spectrometry.idea: Estimate carbon atoms with $n_C\approx\frac{I_{M+1}}{I_M}\times\frac{100}{1.1}$, where $I$ is peak height. For halogens, compare $M:M+2$: one chlorine gives about $3:1$ and one bromine about $1:1$; two chlorines give $M:M+2:M+4\approx9:6:1$, and two bromines about $1:2:1$.
SEM-9701-mass-spectrometry.why: Each carbon contributes about $1.1\%$ to $M+1$ through its heavier isotope; the halogen patterns reflect the relative abundances of their isotopes. These are approximations for a molecular-ion cluster when the relevant peaks are resolved and other isotopes make no substantial contribution to the peaks being compared.
steps: Locate the molecular-ion peak $M$ and the adjacent isotope peaks.
For carbon, divide the $M+1$ height by the $M$ height and apply the formula.
For halogens, compare the heights at $M$, $M+2$ and, if present, $M+4$.
Check that the estimated carbon count is near a whole number or that the halogen ratio fits.

worked.question: A compound has a molecular-ion peak $M$ of height $80.0$ and an $M+1$ peak of height $4.40$. Assume the $M+1$ contribution is mainly from carbon. Estimate the number of carbon atoms.
worked.long: The $M+1$ peak is $4.40/80.0=5.50\%$ of $M$. At about $1.1\%$ per carbon, this corresponds to $5$ carbon atoms.
worked.saving: The ratio converts the two peak heights directly into a carbon estimate.

pitfalls: Using the absolute $M+1$ height without dividing by the $M$ height.
Applying the carbon estimate when another isotope contributes substantially to $M+1$.
Mistaking a two-chlorine $9:6:1$ cluster for a one-bromine $1:1$ pair.
SEM-9701-mass-spectrometry.check: A carbon estimate should be near a whole number; a proposed two-halogen pattern should include an $M+4$ peak.

practice.stem: A compound has molecular-ion peak $M$ of height $200$ and $M+1$ of height $13.2$. Assume the $M+1$ contribution is mainly from carbon. Estimate the number of carbon atoms as a whole number.
hints: Use the height of $M+1$ relative to $M$.
Convert that ratio to a percentage.
Divide the percentage by the approximate contribution per carbon, $1.1\%$.
practice.explanation: $n_C\approx\frac{13.2}{200}\times\frac{100}{1.1}=6$. The answer is $6$.
practice.shortcut_use: Convert the $M+1$ to $M$ height ratio directly to a carbon count.

practice.stem: A molecular-ion cluster has peaks at $M$, $M+2$ and $M+4$ with respective heights $45$, $30$ and $5$. Assume other isotopes make no substantial contribution. Which halogen content best matches the cluster?
hints: The $M+4$ peak makes this a three-peak pattern.
Reduce the three heights to their simplest ratio.
Compare that ratio with the two-chlorine and two-bromine patterns.
practice.explanation: The heights reduce as $45:30:5=9:6:1$, the two-chlorine pattern. The answer is two chlorine atoms.
practice.shortcut_use: Match the reduced three-peak ratio to the halogen pattern.

recall.q: How can $M+1$ and $M$ heights estimate the number of carbon atoms?
recall.a: Multiply their height ratio by $100/1.1$ when $M+1$ is mainly due to carbon.

recall.q: What $M:M+2$ ratios suggest one chlorine or one bromine atom?
recall.a: About $3:1$ suggests chlorine, while about $1:1$ suggests bromine.

recall.q: What three-peak ratios suggest two chlorine or two bromine atoms?
recall.a: The $M:M+2:M+4$ ratios are about $9:6:1$ for two chlorines and $1:2:1$ for two bromines.

SEM-9701-boiling-point-reasoning-templat.hook: A boiling-point explanation can lose its logic when it names a strong bond that boiling does not break.
SEM-9701-boiling-point-reasoning-templat.when: You must compare or explain boiling points from bonding and structure.
SEM-9701-boiling-point-reasoning-templat.idea: State the force or bond overcome, compare its strength, then state the energy needed.
SEM-9701-boiling-point-reasoning-templat.why: Boiling separates particles. For simple molecular substances this overcomes intermolecular forces; for ionic or giant covalent structures it overcomes bonds in the structure, assuming the substances boil without decomposing.
steps: Identify each structure.
Name the relevant intermolecular force or bond.
Compare its strength.
Link greater strength to more energy and a higher boiling point.

worked.question: Methane boils at $-161.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and water at $100\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Explain why water has the higher boiling point.
worked.long: Describe the bonds and forces in both substances, then decide which interactions between molecules must be overcome during boiling.
worked.short: Both are simple molecular. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds; methane molecules have London dispersion forces. More energy is needed to overcome the stronger intermolecular forces in water, so its boiling point is higher.
worked.saving: The structure-to-force-to-energy order avoids claiming that covalent bonds break.

pitfalls: Saying that boiling simple molecular substances breaks covalent bonds within molecules.
Naming a force without linking its strength to energy needed.
Treating an ionic lattice as separate molecules held by intermolecular forces.
SEM-9701-boiling-point-reasoning-templat.check: For a simple molecular substance, the explanation should describe forces between molecules.

practice.stem: Which explanation best accounts for water having a higher boiling point than methane?

options.A: Water has stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate its molecules.
options.B: Water has stronger covalent bonds, which must break during boiling.
options.C: Methane has ionic bonds that need less energy to break.
options.D: Water has fewer electrons, so its molecules cannot separate.

hints: Both substances are simple molecular.
Ask what is overcome when molecules separate.
Compare hydrogen bonds between water molecules with dispersion forces between methane molecules.
practice.explanation: Water has hydrogen bonds between molecules, which are stronger than the dispersion forces between methane molecules; more energy is needed to separate water molecules. The answer is the explanation naming stronger intermolecular forces.
practice.shortcut_use: Follow force, strength, then energy.

practice.stem: A simple molecular substance boils without decomposing. What kind of attraction is overcome between its particles?
hints: Identify the stated structure.
Boiling separates whole molecules.
Name the attractions between molecules.
practice.explanation: Boiling separates molecules while their internal covalent bonds remain, so intermolecular forces are overcome.
practice.shortcut_use: Identify the structure before naming the attraction.

recall.q: What three links make a concise boiling-point explanation?
recall.a: Name the force or bond, compare its strength, then link that strength to energy needed.

recall.q: What is overcome when a simple molecular substance boils without decomposing?
recall.a: Intermolecular forces between molecules.

SEM-9701-polarity.hook: Spotting polar bonds alone can give the wrong answer for a symmetric molecule.
SEM-9701-polarity.when: You are asked whether a molecule with polar bonds is polar overall.
SEM-9701-polarity.idea: Check whether its bond dipoles cancel in the molecular shape; symmetric arrangements of identical outer atoms can cancel.
SEM-9701-polarity.why: Bond dipoles are directional. Their vector sum is zero when the full arrangement makes them cancel, as in $\mathrm{CO_2}$ or $\mathrm{CCl_4}$; an asymmetric arrangement may leave a net dipole.
steps: Identify the polar bonds.
Determine the molecular shape.
Check whether the bond dipoles cancel.
State whether a net dipole remains.

worked.question: Carbon dioxide has two polar C–O bonds and a linear O–C–O shape. Is $\mathrm{CO_2}$ polar overall?
worked.long: Draw the two equal C–O bond dipoles in opposite directions and add them as vectors.
worked.short: The linear molecule has identical bonds on opposite sides, so the dipoles cancel. $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is non-polar overall.
worked.saving: The shape check prevents equating polar bonds with a polar molecule.

pitfalls: Calling every molecule with polar bonds polar.
Assuming any symmetric-looking shape cancels when outer atoms differ.
Ignoring the effect of lone pairs on molecular shape.
SEM-9701-polarity.check: If equal dipoles point in exactly opposite directions, their net dipole is zero.

practice.stem: Which molecule is non-polar overall despite having polar bonds?
hints: Look for a shape that makes bond dipoles cancel.
Check whether the outer atoms are identical.
A tetrahedral molecule with four identical outer atoms has cancelling bond dipoles.
practice.explanation: $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ has four identical C–Cl bonds arranged tetrahedrally, so their dipoles cancel and it is non-polar overall.
practice.shortcut_use: Test symmetry of the bond dipoles.

practice.stem: $\mathrm{BF_3}$ has three identical polar B–F bonds arranged symmetrically in a trigonal planar shape. Is the molecule polar or non-polar overall?
hints: The bonds are polar, but the question concerns the whole molecule.
Use the stated shape to check cancellation.
Three equal bond dipoles point symmetrically around the central atom.
practice.explanation: The three B–F dipoles cancel in the symmetric trigonal planar shape, so $\mathrm{BF_3}$ is non-polar overall.
practice.shortcut_use: Check whether the dipoles cancel in the stated shape.

recall.q: What must you check after identifying polar bonds?
recall.a: Check the molecular shape to see whether the bond dipoles cancel.

recall.q: Why is $\mathrm{CO_2}$ non-polar overall?
recall.a: Its two equal C–O bond dipoles oppose and cancel in a linear shape.

SEM-9701-sigma-and-pi-counting.hook: Counting every line in a multiple bond as the same kind of bond overcounts sigma bonds.
SEM-9701-sigma-and-pi-counting.when: A displayed structure contains single, double or triple bonds and asks for sigma and pi counts.
SEM-9701-sigma-and-pi-counting.idea: Each bonded atom pair has one $\sigma$ bond; a double bond adds one $\pi$, and a triple bond adds two $\pi$.
SEM-9701-sigma-and-pi-counting.why: The first bond between a pair is $\sigma$; extra bonds in ordinary double and triple bonds are $\pi$. For benzene, count its $12$ $\sigma$ bonds and describe its $\pi$ electrons as delocalised.
steps: Count each bonded atom pair once for $\sigma$.
Add one $\pi$ for each double bond.
Add two $\pi$ for each triple bond.
Treat benzene's $\pi$ system as delocalised.

worked.question: Propene has structure $\mathrm{CH_2=CH-CH_3}$. How many $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds does it have?
worked.long: Count six C–H bonds, one C–C single bond and the two components of the C=C double bond.
worked.short: There are eight bonded atom pairs, hence $8\sigma$; the one double bond adds $1\pi$.
worked.saving: One sigma count per atom pair prevents counting the double bond twice as sigma.

pitfalls: Counting a double bond as two $\sigma$ bonds.
Forgetting the C–H $\sigma$ bonds.
Describing benzene's $\pi$ system as three isolated double bonds.
SEM-9701-sigma-and-pi-counting.check: The $\sigma$ count equals the number of bonded atom pairs in the stated structure.

practice.stem: Ethyne has structure $\mathrm{H-C\equiv C-H}$. State its numbers of $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds.
hints: Count bonded atom pairs first.
The C–C triple bond contains one $\sigma$ bond.
Count the two C–H pairs, then add the triple bond's $\pi$ components.
practice.explanation: Two C–H pairs and one C–C pair give $3\sigma$ bonds. The C–C triple bond adds $2\pi$ bonds, so the answer is $3\sigma$ and $2\pi$.
practice.shortcut_use: Count one $\sigma$ per bonded atom pair.

practice.stem: Ethene has structure $\mathrm{CH_2=CH_2}$. State its numbers of $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds.
hints: Count each bonded atom pair once.
Include all four C–H bonds.
The C=C pair contributes one $\sigma$ and one $\pi$.
practice.explanation: Four C–H pairs plus one C–C pair give $5\sigma$ bonds; the double bond adds $1\pi$ bond. The answer is $5\sigma$ and $1\pi$.
practice.shortcut_use: Add $\pi$ bonds only for the extra components of a multiple bond.

recall.q: What does a double bond contain?
recall.a: One $\sigma$ bond and one $\pi$ bond.

recall.q: What does a triple bond contain?
recall.a: One $\sigma$ bond and two $\pi$ bonds.

recall.q: How should benzene's $\pi$ bonding be described?
recall.a: It has a delocalised $\pi$ system.

SEM-9701-dalton-s-law.hook: Reworking the gas equation for every component takes extra steps and invites a wrong total.
SEM-9701-dalton-s-law.when: A gas mixture gives mole amounts or mole fractions and its total pressure.
SEM-9701-dalton-s-law.why: In an ideal gas mixture whose gases share the same volume and temperature, each gas's pressure is proportional to its mole amount; the partial pressures sum to the total pressure.
steps: Find the total number of moles.
Divide the component's moles by the total to get $x_i$.
Multiply $x_i$ by total pressure.
Check that all partial pressures sum to the total.

worked.question: An ideal gas mixture contains $2.0$ mol of nitrogen and $3.0$ mol of oxygen at a total pressure of $100$ kPa. Find the nitrogen partial pressure.
worked.long: At common temperature and volume, pressure is proportional to moles. Split $100$ kPa in the ratio $2:3$, giving nitrogen $40$ kPa.
worked.saving: The mole fraction gives the pressure share directly.

pitfalls: Using the component moles without dividing by total moles.
Adding mole fractions to a pressure instead of multiplying.
Applying the ideal-mixture relation where gases do not behave ideally.
SEM-9701-dalton-s-law.check: The oxygen pressure is $60$ kPa, and $40+60=100$ kPa.

practice.stem: An ideal gas mixture contains $1.0$ mol of helium and $4.0$ mol of neon at a total pressure of $250$ kPa. Find helium's partial pressure in kPa, as an exact number.
hints: Use the component's share of total moles.
Find helium's mole fraction.
practice.explanation: Helium's mole fraction is $1.0/5.0=0.20$, so its partial pressure is $0.20\times250=50$ kPa. The answer is $50$.
practice.shortcut_use: Multiply mole fraction by total pressure.

practice.stem: An ideal gas mixture contains $0.30$ mol of gas A and $0.70$ mol of gas B. Its total pressure is $120$ kPa. Find the partial pressure of gas B in kPa, as an exact number.
hints: The mole amounts sum to a convenient total.
Find gas B's mole fraction.
practice.explanation: Gas B's mole fraction is $0.70/1.00=0.70$, so its partial pressure is $0.70\times120=84$ kPa. The answer is $84$.
practice.shortcut_use: Use gas B's mole fraction as its pressure fraction.

recall.q: How do you obtain a component's partial pressure from its mole fraction?
recall.a: Multiply its mole fraction by the total pressure.

recall.q: What do the partial pressures add up to?
recall.a: They add up to the total pressure.

SEM-9701-born-haber-cycle.hook: A lattice-energy calculation is easy to reverse in sign if the cycle is kept only in your head.
SEM-9701-born-haber-cycle.when: You have formation enthalpy, atomisation, ionisation, electron affinity and need lattice formation enthalpy for a $1:1$ ionic solid $\mathrm{MX}$.
SEM-9701-born-haber-cycle.idea: Write $\Delta H_f=\Delta H_{\mathrm{at}}(\mathrm M)+\mathrm{IE}+\frac{1}{2}D(\mathrm{X_2})+\mathrm{EA}+\Delta H_{\mathrm{latt}}$, then isolate lattice energy on the bottom line.
SEM-9701-born-haber-cycle.why: Hess's law makes the direct formation route equal the route through gaseous atoms and ions. This form holds for $\mathrm{MX}$ made from $\mathrm M$ and $\mathrm{X_2}$, with first ionisation energy, first electron affinity and lattice enthalpy defined for formation from gaseous ions.
steps: Write the formation equation and the gaseous-ion route.
Add atomisation, ionisation, half the $\mathrm{X_2}$ bond dissociation enthalpy, and electron affinity.
Set their sum plus lattice formation enthalpy equal to $\Delta H_f$.
Rearrange for lattice formation enthalpy and check its sign.

worked.question: For $\mathrm{NaCl(s)}$, use $\Delta H_f=-411$, Na atomisation $=+108$, Na first ionisation $=+496$, Cl–Cl bond dissociation $=+242$, and Cl first electron affinity $=-349$, all in kJ mol$^{-1}$. Find lattice formation enthalpy.
worked.long: The gaseous-ion route before lattice formation is $108+496+242/2-349=376$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. To finish at $-411$, lattice formation must contribute $-787$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
worked.saving: Putting lattice formation last fixes its sign when rearranging.

pitfalls: Using the full $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ bond dissociation enthalpy instead of half.
Treating electron affinity as positive when the stated value is negative.
Reporting the lattice dissociation enthalpy when asked for lattice formation enthalpy.
SEM-9701-born-haber-cycle.check: The positive gaseous-ion total, $376$, plus $-787$ gives the stated formation enthalpy, $-411$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

practice.stem: For $\mathrm{KBr(s)}$, $\Delta H_f=-394$, K atomisation $=+89$, K first ionisation $=+419$, Br–Br bond dissociation $=+193$, and Br first electron affinity $=-325$, all in kJ mol$^{-1}$. Find lattice formation enthalpy in kJ mol$^{-1}$, to the nearest $0.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
hints: Lattice formation is the final step from gaseous ions.
Use half the Br–Br bond dissociation enthalpy.
practice.explanation: The steps before lattice formation sum to $89+419+96.5-325=279.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Thus $\Delta H_{\mathrm{latt}}=-394-279.5=-673.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$; the answer is $-673.5$.
practice.shortcut_use: Leave lattice formation as the unknown final term.

practice.stem: For $\mathrm{LiF(s)}$, $\Delta H_f=-617$, Li atomisation $=+161$, Li first ionisation $=+520$, F–F bond dissociation $=+158$, and F first electron affinity $=-328$, all in kJ mol$^{-1}$. Find lattice formation enthalpy in kJ mol$^{-1}$, as an exact number.
hints: Start with the direct formation enthalpy.
Use half the F–F bond dissociation enthalpy.
practice.explanation: The gaseous-ion route before lattice formation sums to $161+520+79-328=432$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Hence $\Delta H_{\mathrm{latt}}=-617-432=-1049$ kJ mol$^{-1}$; the answer is $-1049$.
practice.shortcut_use: Solve for the last term in the Hess cycle.

recall.q: What is the final step when finding lattice formation enthalpy in this cycle?
recall.a: Gaseous ions form the solid ionic lattice.

recall.q: Why is half the $\mathrm{X_2}$ bond dissociation enthalpy used for $\mathrm{MX}$?
recall.a: One mole of $\mathrm{MX}$ needs one mole of X atoms, obtained from half a mole of $\mathrm{X_2}$.

SEM-9701-enthalpy-change-of-solution.hook: The lattice term is often given a negative sign, making it easy to subtract it twice.
SEM-9701-enthalpy-change-of-solution.when: You have lattice formation enthalpy and gaseous-ion hydration enthalpies, and need solution enthalpy.
SEM-9701-enthalpy-change-of-solution.why: The lattice enthalpy here is for gaseous ions forming the solid; dissolving reverses that step. Hess's law then adds hydration of the gaseous ions. This holds for the stated lattice formation and hydration definitions and the ions in the dissolution equation.
steps: Write the solid-to-gaseous-ions step as the negative of lattice formation enthalpy.
Add each ion's hydration enthalpy with its equation coefficient.
Sum to obtain solution enthalpy.
Check the sign against the two route totals.

worked.question: For $\mathrm{NaCl(s)\rightarrow Na^+(aq)+Cl^-(aq)}$, lattice formation enthalpy is $-787$ kJ mol$^{-1}$; hydration enthalpies are Na$^+$ $=-406$ and Cl$^-$ $=-381$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Find the enthalpy change of solution.
worked.long: Reverse lattice formation to separate the solid into gaseous ions: $+787$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Hydrate the ions: $-406-381=-787$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. The net is $0$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
worked.saving: Reversing the lattice arrow once prevents a double sign change.

pitfalls: Adding the negative lattice formation value without reversing it.
Using hydration enthalpy for only one ion.
Ignoring ion coefficients when more than one of an ion is produced.
SEM-9701-enthalpy-change-of-solution.check: The stated lattice separation and total hydration values are equal and opposite, so the result is zero.

practice.stem: For $\mathrm{KCl(s)\rightarrow K^+(aq)+Cl^-(aq)}$, lattice formation enthalpy is $-717$ kJ mol$^{-1}$; hydration enthalpies are K$^+$ $=-322$ and Cl$^-$ $=-381$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Find solution enthalpy in kJ mol$^{-1}$, as an exact number.
hints: The stated lattice value is for formation.
Reverse that step before adding hydration.
practice.explanation: Lattice separation is $+717$ and hydration totals $-703$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Thus solution enthalpy is $717-703=+14$ kJ mol$^{-1}$; the answer is $14$.
practice.shortcut_use: Negate lattice formation enthalpy once.

practice.stem: For $\mathrm{CaCl_2(s)\rightarrow Ca^{2+}(aq)+2Cl^-(aq)}$, lattice formation enthalpy is $-2258$ kJ mol$^{-1}$; hydration enthalpies are Ca$^{2+}$ $=-1577$ and Cl$^-$ $=-381$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Find solution enthalpy in kJ mol$^{-1}$, as an exact number.
hints: Reverse the lattice formation step.
The dissolution equation produces two chloride ions.
practice.explanation: Lattice separation is $+2258$ and hydration totals $-1577-2\times381=-2339$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Thus solution enthalpy is $2258-2339=-81$ kJ mol$^{-1}$; the answer is $-81$.
practice.shortcut_use: Use the ion coefficients in the hydration sum.

recall.q: What sign does a lattice formation enthalpy take when the solid separates into gaseous ions?
recall.a: Its sign is reversed.

recall.q: How is solution enthalpy found from lattice formation and hydration enthalpies?
recall.a: Negate lattice formation enthalpy and add the hydration enthalpies for all ions produced.

SEM-9701-molecular-formula.hook: Writing out possible multiples of an empirical formula takes time and makes subscripts easy to miss.
SEM-9701-molecular-formula.when: The question gives an empirical formula and the compound’s relative molecular mass, $M_r$.
SEM-9701-molecular-formula.idea: Divide $M_r$ by the empirical formula mass to get $k$. Multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by $k$.
SEM-9701-molecular-formula.why: The molecular formula contains a whole number of empirical formula units, so this works when the stated empirical formula and $M_r$ describe the same compound. Then $k$ is a whole number.
steps: Calculate the empirical formula mass.
Find $k$ by dividing $M_r$ by that mass.
Multiply every empirical subscript by $k$.

worked.question: A compound has empirical formula $\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{O}$ and $M_r=180$. Use relative atomic masses $\mathrm{C}=12$, $\mathrm{H}=1$ and $\mathrm{O}=16$. Find its molecular formula.
worked.long: Write the formula as $\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}\mathrm{O}_n$. Its mass is $12n+2n+16n=30n$, so $30n=180$ and $n=6$.
worked.short: The empirical formula mass is $12+2+16=30$, so $k=180/30=6$. The molecular formula is $\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O}_6$.
worked.saving: One division replaces solving for the repeated subscript.

pitfalls: Multiplying only one subscript: every atom count must be multiplied by $k$.
Using an atomic mass in place of the mass of the entire empirical formula.
Rounding a value of $k$ that is far from a whole number instead of checking the data.
SEM-9701-molecular-formula.check: Add the atomic masses in the proposed molecular formula; they must give the stated $M_r$.

practice.stem: A compound has empirical formula $\mathrm{CH}$ and $M_r=78$. Use relative atomic masses $\mathrm{C}=12$ and $\mathrm{H}=1$. Give its molecular formula.
hints: You have an empirical formula and $M_r$.
Find the mass of one empirical formula unit, then divide $M_r$ by it.
Use $k=78/(12+1)$ and multiply both subscripts by $k$.
practice.explanation: The empirical formula mass is $12+1=13$, so $k=78/13=6$. Multiplying both subscripts gives $\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_6$.
practice.shortcut_use: Divide $M_r$ by the empirical formula mass.

practice.stem: A compound has empirical formula $\mathrm{N}\mathrm{O}_2$ and $M_r=92$. Use relative atomic masses $\mathrm{N}=14$ and $\mathrm{O}=16$. Give its molecular formula.
hints: The given formula is empirical.
Include both oxygen atoms when finding its formula mass.
Use $k=92/(14+2\times16)$, then multiply each subscript by $k$.
practice.explanation: The empirical formula mass is $14+2\times16=46$, so $k=92/46=2$. Multiplying both atom counts gives $\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4$.
practice.shortcut_use: Use the whole empirical formula mass to find $k$.

recall.q: How do you find the number of empirical formula units in a molecule?
recall.a: Divide $M_r$ by the empirical formula mass.

recall.q: Which subscripts change when converting an empirical formula to a molecular formula?
recall.a: Multiply every subscript by the same whole number $k$.

SEM-9701-percentage-yield-and-atom-econo.hook: Both calculations produce a percentage, but they compare different quantities. Mixing up the denominators gives a plausible wrong answer.
SEM-9701-percentage-yield-and-atom-econo.when: Use percentage yield when actual and theoretical amounts of product are given. Use atom economy when a balanced equation identifies a desired product and the other products.
SEM-9701-percentage-yield-and-atom-econo.idea: Percentage yield is $100\times A/T$, where $A$ is actual yield and $T$ is theoretical yield. Atom economy is $100\times D/P$, where $D$ is the formula mass of the desired product multiplied by its coefficient, and $P$ is the sum of formula masses of all products multiplied by their coefficients.
SEM-9701-percentage-yield-and-atom-econo.why: Yield compares what was obtained with the maximum predicted amount; use the same product and units for $A$ and $T$. Atom economy compares desired product mass with total product mass in the balanced equation; count every product coefficient.
steps: Identify whether the question asks about an actual yield or a balanced equation’s products.
For yield, divide actual by theoretical and multiply by $100$.
For atom economy, multiply each product’s formula mass by its coefficient.
Divide the desired product’s contribution by the total, then multiply by $100$.

worked.question: Calcium carbonate decomposes to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, with one mole of each product formed per mole of calcium carbonate. The theoretical yield of calcium oxide is $11.2$ g, and the actual yield is $8.96$ g. Find the percentage yield of calcium oxide and its atom economy. Use relative atomic masses $\mathrm{Ca}=40$, $\mathrm{C}=12$ and $\mathrm{O}=16$.
worked.long: The actual yield is $8.96/11.2=0.80$ of the theoretical yield, or $80\%$. The products have formula masses $56$ and $44$, totalling $100$; calcium oxide accounts for $56/100=0.56$, or $56\%$.
worked.saving: Using the two ratios directly avoids mixing the actual yield into the atom economy calculation.

pitfalls: Dividing theoretical yield by actual yield.
Using reactant masses or actual yield in the atom economy denominator.
Ignoring a product coefficient when adding product formula masses.
SEM-9701-percentage-yield-and-atom-econo.check: Both percentages should lie between $0\%$ and $100\%$ for these stated quantities.

practice.stem: The theoretical yield of a product is $15.0$ g and the actual yield is $13.5$ g. Find the percentage yield, in %, as an exact whole number.
hints: The question gives actual and theoretical yields.
Put actual yield over theoretical yield.
Calculate $100\times13.5/15.0$.
practice.explanation: Percentage yield $=100\times13.5/15.0=90\%$. The answer is $90$.
practice.shortcut_use: Apply the actual-to-theoretical ratio directly.

practice.stem: Two moles of hydrogen peroxide decompose to two moles of water and one mole of oxygen. Find the atom economy for oxygen, in %, to $3$ significant figures. Use $M_r(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})=18$ and $M_r(\mathrm{O}_2)=32$.
hints: Oxygen is the desired product; water is the other product.
Count the two moles of water in the total product mass.
Calculate $100\times32/(2\times18+32)$.
practice.explanation: The desired product contributes $32$ mass units and all products contribute $2\times18+32=68$. Atom economy $=100\times32/68\approx47.1\%$. The answer is $47.1$.
practice.shortcut_use: Use coefficient-weighted product masses in the ratio.

recall.q: What goes in the denominator of percentage yield?
recall.a: The theoretical yield of the same product, in the same units as the actual yield.

recall.q: What goes in the denominator of atom economy?
recall.a: The total formula mass of all products, counting their coefficients in the balanced equation.

recall.q: Does actual yield affect atom economy?
recall.a: No; atom economy uses the products and coefficients in the balanced equation.

SEM-9701-entropy.hook: Comparing every possible arrangement is slow. For a reaction, gas mole counts often reveal the likely entropy direction at once.
SEM-9701-entropy.when: You are asked to predict the sign of the system entropy change, or given standard molar entropies for a reaction.
SEM-9701-entropy.idea: More moles of gas usually mean a positive $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}$. For a numerical value, use $\Delta S^\circ=\sum S^\circ(\mathrm{products})-\sum S^\circ(\mathrm{reactants})$, including stoichiometric coefficients.
SEM-9701-entropy.why: Gas particles have many more available arrangements than particles in liquids or solids. The gas mole shortcut is a qualitative guide when gas production or consumption dominates other changes; the standard entropy formula applies when the listed values and the reaction refer to the same standard conditions.
steps: Count gaseous moles on each side.
Predict the sign if the gas change dominates.
For a value, multiply each $S^\circ$ by its coefficient.
Subtract the reactant total from the product total.

worked.question: For $\mathrm{N_2(g)+3H_2(g)\to 2NH_3(g)}$, the standard molar entropies of $\mathrm{N_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2}$ and $\mathrm{NH_3}$ are 192, 131 and 193 J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$, respectively. Predict the sign and calculate $\Delta S^\circ$ in J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ of reaction.
worked.long: Add the reactant entropies: $192+3(131)=585$. Add the product entropies: $2(193)=386$. Hence $\Delta S^\circ=386-585=-199$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$.
worked.short: Four gas moles become two, so expect a negative sign. Then $\Delta S^\circ=2(193)-[192+3(131)]=-199$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$.
worked.saving: The gas count gives a sign check before the arithmetic.

pitfalls: Counting molecules without applying the balanced coefficients.
Treating the gas mole rule as an exact calculation when other entropy changes matter.
Reversing products and reactants in the subtraction.
SEM-9701-entropy.check: The calculated sign is negative, matching the fall from four to two gas moles.

practice.stem: For $\mathrm{A(g)\to 2B(g)}$, $S^\circ(\mathrm A)=150$ and $S^\circ(\mathrm B)=120$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$. Find $\Delta S^\circ$ in J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ of reaction, as an integer.
hints: Compare gas moles on the two sides.
Apply the coefficient to the product entropy.
practice.explanation: Gas moles rise from one to two, suggesting a positive value. $\Delta S^\circ=2(120)-150=90$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ of reaction. Answer: 90.
practice.shortcut_use: Gas mole count checks the sign.

practice.stem: For $\mathrm{2C(g)\to D(g)}$, $S^\circ(\mathrm C)=200$ and $S^\circ(\mathrm D)=250$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$. What is $\Delta S^\circ$ in J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ of reaction?
hints: Compare the gas mole counts to anticipate the sign.
Multiply the entropy of $\mathrm C$ by its coefficient.
practice.explanation: Two gas moles become one, so a negative value is plausible. $\Delta S^\circ=250-2(200)=-150$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ of reaction. Answer: $-150$.
practice.shortcut_use: Gas mole count checks the subtraction sign.

recall.q: What gas mole change usually gives a positive system entropy change?
recall.a: An increase in gas moles usually gives positive $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}$ when that change dominates.

recall.q: How is a standard reaction entropy calculated?
recall.a: Subtract the coefficient-weighted reactant entropy total from the coefficient-weighted product total.

SEM-9701-electrolysis-products.hook: Listing every possible electrode reaction wastes time and makes it easy to swap oxidation and reduction.
SEM-9701-electrolysis-products.when: An aqueous electrolysis question asks which substances form at the cathode and anode.
SEM-9701-electrolysis-products.idea: Use “AN OX, RED CAT”: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. At the cathode, $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ is reduced in preference to hydrogen ions, while hydrogen forms in preference to sodium. At the anode, concentrated chloride gives $\mathrm{Cl_2}$; dilute chloride gives $\mathrm{O_2}$.
SEM-9701-electrolysis-products.why: Reduction gains electrons and oxidation loses them; this electrode assignment always holds for electrolysis. The product comparisons here apply to the specified aqueous ions, with chloride concentration affecting the anode product.
steps: Identify the ions and water present.
Assign reduction to the cathode and oxidation to the anode.
Use the competing species to choose the cathode product.
For chloride solution, use its concentration to choose the anode product.

worked.question: An aqueous, concentrated $\mathrm{NaCl}$ solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. State the gas formed at each electrode.
worked.long: List possible reductions of sodium ions and water and possible oxidations of chloride and water; compare each pair.
worked.short: “RED CAT” gives hydrogen at the cathode in preference to sodium. “AN OX” and concentrated chloride give chlorine at the anode. The gases are $\mathrm{H_2}$ and $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, respectively.
worked.saving: The electrode mnemonic prevents anode and cathode products being interchanged.

pitfalls: Putting oxidation at the cathode.
Predicting sodium metal from aqueous $\mathrm{NaCl}$.
Using the concentrated chloride anode product for dilute chloride.
SEM-9701-electrolysis-products.check: The cathode reaction must consume electrons; the anode reaction must release them.

practice.stem: A dilute aqueous $\mathrm{NaCl}$ solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which gas forms at the cathode and which at the anode?
hints: Identify the solution as dilute and aqueous.
Assign reduction to the cathode and oxidation to the anode.
Hydrogen forms in preference to sodium; use the dilute chloride rule at the anode.
practice.explanation: Reduction at the cathode produces $\mathrm{H_2}$ in preference to sodium. For dilute aqueous chloride, oxidation at the anode produces $\mathrm{O_2}$. Answer: cathode $\mathrm{H_2}$; anode $\mathrm{O_2}$.
practice.shortcut_use: The mnemonic assigns electrodes before product selection.

practice.stem: A concentrated aqueous $\mathrm{NaCl}$ solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Name the anode product.
hints: The solution contains chloride ions.
The anode is the site of oxidation.
Apply the concentrated chloride rule at the anode.
practice.explanation: Concentrated chloride is oxidised at the anode, producing $\mathrm{Cl_2}$. Answer: chlorine.
practice.shortcut_use: The concentration rule selects the anode product.

recall.q: What does “AN OX, RED CAT” mean?
recall.a: Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

recall.q: How does chloride concentration affect the anode product in these aqueous solutions?
recall.a: Concentrated chloride gives chlorine; dilute chloride gives oxygen.

SEM-9701-cancel-a-common-total-pressure.hook: Substituting every partial pressure into $K_p$ creates repeated factors of total pressure that can obscure a simple cancellation.
SEM-9701-cancel-a-common-total-pressure.when: Every species in a gas equilibrium is gaseous, and the total product and reactant stoichiometric coefficients are equal.
SEM-9701-cancel-a-common-total-pressure.idea: Write each partial pressure as $p_i=x_iP$. If $\Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}=0$, all factors of $P$ cancel from $K_p$.
SEM-9701-cancel-a-common-total-pressure.why: The net power of $P$ is $\Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}$, so it is zero here. For an ideal-gas mixture at fixed temperature, changing total pressure alone then leaves the equilibrium composition unchanged.
steps: Count gas coefficients on each side.
Confirm $\Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}=0$.
Replace each $p_i$ with $x_iP$ in $K_p$.
Cancel $P$ before using mole fractions.

worked.question: For $\mathrm{H_2(g)+I_2(g)\rightleftharpoons 2HI(g)}$ at fixed temperature, the equilibrium mole fractions are $x_{\mathrm{H_2}}=0.25$, $x_{\mathrm{I_2}}=0.25$ and $x_{\mathrm{HI}}=0.50$. Treat the mixture as ideal. Find $K_p$.
worked.long: At any total pressure $P$, substitute $p_{\mathrm{H_2}}=0.25P$, $p_{\mathrm{I_2}}=0.25P$ and $p_{\mathrm{HI}}=0.50P$: $K_p=(0.50P)^2/[(0.25P)(0.25P)]=4$.
worked.short: Two gas moles occur on each side, so cancel $P$ first: $K_p=0.50^2/(0.25\times0.25)=4$.
worked.saving: It removes an unnecessary pressure value and its units before calculation.

pitfalls: Cancelling $P$ when $\Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}$ is not zero.
Forgetting to square the mole fraction of a species with coefficient two.
Claiming the composition stays fixed when temperature changes.
SEM-9701-cancel-a-common-total-pressure.check: The mole fractions sum to one, and $K_p$ has no remaining pressure factor.

practice.stem: For ideal gases $\mathrm{A(g)+B(g)\rightleftharpoons 2C(g)}$ at fixed temperature, the equilibrium mole fractions are $x_{\mathrm A}=0.20$, $x_{\mathrm B}=0.20$ and $x_{\mathrm C}=0.60$. Find $K_p$ as an integer.
hints: Count gas coefficients on each side.
Cancel the common total pressure.
practice.explanation: The gas coefficients total two on each side, so $P$ cancels. $K_p=0.60^2/(0.20\times0.20)=9$. Answer: 9.
practice.shortcut_use: Cancel total pressure before inserting mole fractions.

practice.stem: For ideal gases $\mathrm{D(g)+E(g)\rightleftharpoons F(g)+G(g)}$ at fixed temperature, the equilibrium mole fractions are $x_{\mathrm D}=0.10$, $x_{\mathrm E}=0.20$, $x_{\mathrm F}=0.30$ and $x_{\mathrm G}=0.40$. Find $K_p$ as an integer.
hints: Compare the gas coefficient totals.
Use mole fractions after cancelling $P$.
practice.explanation: The gas coefficient totals are equal, so $P$ cancels. $K_p=(0.30\times0.40)/(0.10\times0.20)=6$. Answer: 6.
practice.shortcut_use: Cancel total pressure from the $K_p$ expression.

recall.q: When does total pressure cancel from a gas $K_p$ expression?
recall.a: It cancels when $\Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}=0$.

recall.q: What conditions keep equilibrium composition unchanged when total pressure alone changes?
recall.a: The mixture must behave ideally, temperature must be fixed, and $\Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}=0$.

SEM-9701-how-a-buffer-works.hook: Memorising a vague claim that a buffer resists pH change does not show which component removes an added acid or alkali.
SEM-9701-how-a-buffer-works.when: A question adds a small amount of $\mathrm{H^+}$ or $\mathrm{OH^-}$ to a mixture containing a weak acid $\mathrm{HA}$ and its conjugate base $\mathrm{A^-}$.
SEM-9701-how-a-buffer-works.idea: Added $\mathrm{H^+}$ is removed by $\mathrm{A^-}$: $\mathrm{A^-+H^+\to HA}$. Added $\mathrm{OH^-}$ is removed by $\mathrm{HA}$: $\mathrm{HA+OH^-\to A^-+H_2O}$.
SEM-9701-how-a-buffer-works.why: Each added ion reacts with one member of the conjugate pair. This works as a buffer while both components are present in substantial amounts relative to the addition; capacity is greatest when $[\mathrm{A^-}]=[\mathrm{HA}]$.
steps: Identify whether acid or alkali is added.
Choose $\mathrm{A^-}$ for acid or $\mathrm{HA}$ for alkali.
Write the removal reaction.
Check that enough of that component remains.

worked.question: A buffer contains 0.20 mol $\mathrm{HA}$ and 0.20 mol $\mathrm{A^-}$. Assume volumes are unchanged. What removes 0.010 mol of added $\mathrm{H^+}$, and how many moles of each component remain?
worked.long: Use the reaction stoichiometry: 0.010 mol $\mathrm{A^-}$ reacts with 0.010 mol $\mathrm{H^+}$ to form 0.010 mol $\mathrm{HA}$. Thus $\mathrm{A^-}$ becomes 0.190 mol and $\mathrm{HA}$ becomes 0.210 mol.
worked.short: Acid added means use $\mathrm{A^-}$. Subtract 0.010 mol from $\mathrm{A^-}$ and add it to $\mathrm{HA}$: 0.190 mol and 0.210 mol.
worked.saving: Choosing the reacting member first prevents reversing the mole changes.

pitfalls: Using $\mathrm{HA}$ to remove added $\mathrm{H^+}$.
Calling a mixture a useful buffer when one component has been nearly exhausted.
Assuming equal concentrations are required for any buffering; they give greatest capacity.
SEM-9701-how-a-buffer-works.check: The total amount of $\mathrm{HA}$ plus $\mathrm{A^-}$ remains 0.40 mol in the worked reaction.

practice.stem: A buffer initially contains 0.30 mol $\mathrm{HA}$ and 0.20 mol $\mathrm{A^-}$. Assume volumes are unchanged. After 0.050 mol $\mathrm{OH^-}$ is added and reacts completely, how many moles of $\mathrm{HA}$ remain? Give the answer in mol, to 2 decimal places.
hints: The added species is alkali.
Choose the buffer component that reacts with $\mathrm{OH^-}$.
Subtract $0.050$ mol from the initial $0.30$ mol of $\mathrm{HA}$.
practice.explanation: $\mathrm{HA}$ removes $\mathrm{OH^-}$ in a one-to-one reaction. $0.30-0.050=0.25$ mol $\mathrm{HA}$ remains. Answer: 0.25.
practice.shortcut_use: Match added alkali to $\mathrm{HA}$ immediately.

practice.stem: A buffer contains substantial amounts of $\mathrm{HA}$ and $\mathrm{A^-}$. A small amount of strong acid is added. Which change occurs first?
hints: Identify the ion introduced by the strong acid.
Select the conjugate-base component.
Use $\mathrm{A^-+H^+\to HA}$ to identify the direction of change.
practice.explanation: Added acid supplies $\mathrm{H^+}$, which $\mathrm{A^-}$ removes: $\mathrm{A^-+H^+\to HA}$. Thus $\mathrm{HA}$ increases. Answer: $\mathrm{A^-}$ reacts with $\mathrm{H^+}$, increasing $\mathrm{HA}$.
practice.shortcut_use: Match added acid to $\mathrm{A^-}$ immediately.

recall.q: Which buffer component removes added $\mathrm{H^+}$?
recall.a: The conjugate base $\mathrm{A^-}$ removes it by forming $\mathrm{HA}$.

recall.q: When is buffer capacity greatest for an $\mathrm{HA}/\mathrm{A^-}$ pair?
recall.a: Capacity is greatest when $[\mathrm{A^-}]=[\mathrm{HA}]$.

SEM-9701-indicator-choice-for-a-titratio.hook: An indicator can change colour far from the equivalence point, giving a poor endpoint.
SEM-9701-indicator-choice-for-a-titratio.when: You are given a titration curve or the strengths of the acid and base and must choose an indicator.
SEM-9701-indicator-choice-for-a-titratio.idea: Choose an indicator whose transition range lies inside the steep section of the pH curve. Use methyl orange for strong acid with weak base, phenolphthalein for weak acid with strong base, and either for a typical strong acid with strong base titration.
SEM-9701-indicator-choice-for-a-titratio.why: A steep pH change makes a small volume change cross the indicator range, so its colour change is close to equivalence. This condition fails for a weak acid with weak base titration because there is no sufficiently steep section for these indicators.
steps: Identify whether each reagent is strong or weak.
Locate the steep pH change near equivalence.
Choose an indicator whose range lies in that section.
For weak acid with weak base, reject these visual indicators.

worked.question: 25.0 cm$^3$ of 0.100 mol dm$^{-3}$ ethanoic acid is titrated with 0.100 mol dm$^{-3}$ sodium hydroxide. The steep section near equivalence is above pH 7. Choose methyl orange or phenolphthalein.
worked.long: Inspect the full pH curve and compare both indicator transition ranges with its steep section.
worked.short: Weak acid with strong base has its steep section above pH 7; choose phenolphthalein.
worked.saving: The acid–base pair identifies the suitable range without tracing the whole curve.

pitfalls: Choosing methyl orange for a weak acid with strong base.
Assuming every titration has a sharp enough pH jump for a visual indicator.
Choosing by the initial pH rather than the steep section near equivalence.
SEM-9701-indicator-choice-for-a-titratio.check: The indicator must change colour during the steep pH jump, close to equivalence.

practice.stem: A strong acid is titrated with a weak base. Which indicator is the better choice from the following?
hints: Identify the strong acid and weak base pair.
Locate its steep section on the acidic side.
Choose the indicator whose transition range fits that section.
practice.explanation: The steep section for strong acid with weak base is on the acidic side. Methyl orange changes colour there. Answer: methyl orange.
practice.shortcut_use: Use the acid–base pair to locate the steep section.

practice.stem: A weak acid is titrated with a weak base. Which indicator choice is justified by the pH curve shortcut?
hints: Identify both reagents as weak.
Ask whether the curve has a sufficiently steep section.
Apply the indicator rule for a weak acid with a weak base.
practice.explanation: The weak acid–weak base curve has no sufficiently steep section for either named indicator. Answer: neither methyl orange nor phenolphthalein.
practice.shortcut_use: Recognise the weak–weak pair before choosing an indicator.

recall.q: Where should an indicator transition range lie?
recall.a: It should lie in the steep section of the titration pH curve.

recall.q: Which indicator suits a weak acid titrated with a strong base?
recall.a: Phenolphthalein suits that titration.

SEM-9701-units-of.hook: Memorised units of equilibrium constants are easy to misapply when the reaction coefficients change.
SEM-9701-units-of.when: You are asked for the units of $K_c$ from a balanced concentration expression.
SEM-9701-units-of.idea: Write the $K_c$ expression and combine concentration units using its powers. For gas or solute concentrations in mol dm$^{-3}$, the net power is the product coefficient total minus the reactant coefficient total.
SEM-9701-units-of.why: Every concentration contributes one factor of mol dm$^{-3}$ per power in the expression. This unit bookkeeping always holds for a $K_c$ value defined directly by concentrations expressed in mol dm$^{-3}$; if the net power is zero, the units cancel.
steps: Write the balanced $K_c$ expression.
Count the total powers in numerator and denominator.
Subtract denominator powers from numerator powers.
Apply that net power to mol dm$^{-3}$.

worked.question: For $\mathrm{A+B\rightleftharpoons C}$, concentrations are measured in mol dm$^{-3}$. Give the units of $K_c$.
worked.long: $K_c=[\mathrm C]/([\mathrm A][\mathrm B])$, so its units are $(\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})/(\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})^2=\mathrm{mol^{-1}\,dm^3}$.
worked.short: Product coefficient total is one; reactant total is two. Net power is $-1$, giving mol$^{-1}$ dm$^3$.
worked.saving: Counting powers avoids rearranging the unit fraction each time.

pitfalls: Using the number of species instead of stoichiometric coefficients.
Forgetting that a negative power of dm$^{-3}$ becomes dm$^3$.
Claiming no units whenever the number of distinct species is equal.
SEM-9701-units-of.check: Substitute one mol dm$^{-3}$ factor for every bracket in the $K_c$ expression and confirm the same units.

practice.stem: For $\mathrm{2A\rightleftharpoons B}$, with concentrations in mol dm$^{-3}$, state the units of $K_c$.
hints: Use the balanced coefficients as powers.
Subtract two reactant powers from one product power.
Apply the net power $-1$ to mol dm$^{-3}$.
practice.explanation: $K_c=[\mathrm B]/[\mathrm A]^2$, so the net concentration power is $1-2=-1$. The units are mol$^{-1}$ dm$^3$. Answer: mol$^{-1}$ dm$^3$.
practice.shortcut_use: Count the net concentration power.

practice.stem: For $\mathrm{A+B\rightleftharpoons C+D}$, with concentrations in mol dm$^{-3}$, state the units of $K_c$.
hints: Count the coefficient total on each side.
Compare numerator and denominator powers.
The concentration-unit factor has the same power above and below the fraction.
practice.explanation: The product and reactant coefficient totals are both two, so the concentration units cancel. Answer: no units.
practice.shortcut_use: Equal coefficient totals reveal cancellation.

recall.q: How do you find the units of $K_c$?
recall.a: Apply the net stoichiometric power in its concentration expression to the concentration unit.

recall.q: When do concentration units cancel from $K_c$?
recall.a: They cancel when the total product and reactant coefficient powers are equal.

SEM-9701-maxwell-boltzmann.hook: Redrawing the whole energy distribution can lead to a taller hot curve or a changed area, both of which misrepresent the same sample of molecules.
SEM-9701-maxwell-boltzmann.when: A question compares molecular energy distributions at two temperatures or asks how a catalyst affects the fraction above activation energy $E_a$.
SEM-9701-maxwell-boltzmann.idea: For the same number of molecules, a hotter Maxwell–Boltzmann curve starts at the origin, has the same area, and has a lower peak farther right; more molecules have energy at least $E_a$. A catalyst lowers $E_a$ without changing the curve at fixed temperature.
SEM-9701-maxwell-boltzmann.why: Heating spreads molecular energies over a wider range while the total number of molecules remains fixed. Lowering $E_a$ moves the threshold left, increasing the fraction beyond it; these statements hold for the same sample size, with the catalyst comparison at fixed temperature.
steps: Keep the curve starting at the origin.
For higher temperature, keep its area fixed and lower and shift its peak right.
Compare the area beyond $E_a$.
For a catalyst at fixed temperature, move $E_a$ left and leave the curve unchanged.

worked.question: At one temperature, 10% of 1000 molecules have energy at least $E_a$. A catalyst lowers $E_a$ so that 25% have energy at least the new threshold. How many additional molecules meet the threshold, assuming the temperature and number of molecules stay fixed?
worked.long: The original count is $0.10(1000)=100$ and the new count is $0.25(1000)=250$. The increase is $250-100=150$ molecules.
worked.short: The threshold moves left on the same curve. The extra fraction is $25\%-10\%=15\%$, so $0.15(1000)=150$ molecules.
worked.saving: Comparing shaded fractions avoids redrawing or altering the distribution.

pitfalls: Raising the peak of the hotter curve while keeping its area unchanged.
Changing the curve itself when only a catalyst is added at fixed temperature.
Shading below $E_a$ instead of above it.
SEM-9701-maxwell-boltzmann.check: For a fixed number of molecules, the area under either distribution must represent the same total.

practice.stem: At fixed temperature, 8% of 500 molecules have energy at least $E_a$. A catalyst lowers $E_a$, after which 20% meet the threshold. How many additional molecules meet the threshold? Give an integer.
hints: The catalyst changes the threshold, not the distribution.
Find the increase in the fraction above the threshold.
Calculate $(0.20-0.08)\times500$.
practice.explanation: The added fraction is $20\%-8\%=12\%$. Thus $0.12(500)=60$ additional molecules meet the threshold. Answer: 60.
practice.shortcut_use: Subtract the fractions above the two thresholds.

practice.stem: Two Maxwell–Boltzmann energy curves represent the same number of molecules at different temperatures. Which description fits the higher-temperature curve?

options.A: Higher peak farther right, with greater area
options.B: Lower peak farther right, with the same area
options.C: Lower peak farther left, with the same area

hints: The sample contains the same number of molecules.
Keep the area under the two curves equal.
Heating spreads energies, lowering the peak and moving it towards higher energy.
practice.explanation: The same number of molecules gives the same area. At higher temperature the distribution spreads, so its peak is lower and farther right. Answer: lower peak farther right, with the same area.
practice.shortcut_use: Preserve area while shifting and lowering the hot peak.

recall.q: How do peak position, peak height and area change on heating the same sample?
recall.a: The peak moves right and lowers, while the area stays the same.

recall.q: What does a catalyst change on a Maxwell–Boltzmann energy diagram at fixed temperature?
recall.a: It lowers $E_a$, leaving the distribution curve unchanged.

SEM-9701-disproportionation.hook: Trying to memorise separate oxidation and reduction reactions takes time. Oxidation numbers show both changes in one equation.
SEM-9701-disproportionation.when: The same element in one reactant appears in two products with different oxidation numbers.
SEM-9701-disproportionation.idea: Assign oxidation numbers to that element. If one increases and the other decreases, it disproportionates.
SEM-9701-disproportionation.why: This test always holds because oxidation is an increase in oxidation number and reduction is a decrease. Both must happen to the same element in the same reaction.
steps: Find the element present in both products.
Assign its oxidation number in the reactant and each product.
Check for one increase and one decrease.

worked.question: Chlorine reacts with cold, dilute sodium hydroxide: $\mathrm{Cl_2}+2\mathrm{NaOH}$ → $\mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{NaClO}+\mathrm{H_2O}$. Show that chlorine disproportionates.
worked.long: Write separate oxidation and reduction half equations, then combine them.
worked.short: Chlorine is $0$ in $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, $-1$ in $\mathrm{NaCl}$ and $+1$ in $\mathrm{NaClO}$. It is both reduced and oxidised.
worked.saving: Three oxidation numbers replace two half equations.

pitfalls: Calling a reaction disproportionation when different elements are oxidised and reduced.
Assigning chlorine $+1$ in $\mathrm{NaCl}$ instead of $-1$.
SEM-9701-disproportionation.check: The reactant oxidation number must lie between the two product oxidation numbers.

practice.stem: Chlorine reacts with water: $\mathrm{Cl_2}+\mathrm{H_2O}$ ⇌ $\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{HClO}$. Which pair gives the oxidation numbers of chlorine in the two products?
hints: Chlorine appears in both products.
Assign its oxidation number in each compound.
Use hydrogen as $+1$ and oxygen as $-2$.
practice.explanation: In $\mathrm{HCl}$, chlorine is $-1$; in $\mathrm{HClO}$, it is $+1$. The answer is $-1$ and $+1$.
practice.shortcut_use: Compare chlorine oxidation numbers directly.

practice.stem: In the hot reaction $3\mathrm{Cl_2}+6\mathrm{NaOH}$ → $5\mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{NaClO_3}+3\mathrm{H_2O}$, what is the oxidation number of chlorine in $\mathrm{NaClO_3}$? Give a bare integer.
hints: The chlorine-containing products have different oxidation numbers.
Use the total charge of the chlorate ion.
Set the chlorine oxidation number plus $3(-2)$ equal to $-1$.
practice.explanation: For $\mathrm{ClO_3^-}$, chlorine has oxidation number $x$ where $x+3(-2)=-1$, so $x=+5$. The answer is $5$.
practice.shortcut_use: Assign the product oxidation number directly.

recall.q: What identifies disproportionation?
recall.a: The same element is both oxidised and reduced in one reaction.

recall.q: What oxidation number changes occur?
recall.a: One product has a higher oxidation number and another a lower one than the reactant.

SEM-9701-period-3-chlorides.hook: Treating every Period 3 chloride as behaving like sodium chloride in water gives the wrong acidity and products.
SEM-9701-period-3-chlorides.when: A question asks what happens when a Period 3 chloride meets water.
SEM-9701-period-3-chlorides.idea: Identify the chloride first: $\mathrm{NaCl}$ dissolves to a neutral solution; $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ gives a slightly acidic solution; $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ hydrolyses; $\mathrm{SiCl_4}$ and $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ hydrolyse fully, producing $\mathrm{HCl}$ and an oxo-acid.
